newsitem.title: FRANCE: French officials dismiss talk of early election.
newsitem.headline: French officials dismiss talk of early election.

text.p: French officials dismissed press reports on Thursday that President Jacques Chirac might dissolve parliament and call an early general election this year.

Reports in the newspapers Liberation and Le Monde quoted unnamed cabinet ministers and aides to Prime Minister Alain Juppe as saying the chances of winning an election might be better this June than next March, when the poll is due.
But one government official said: "There is no factual basis for such rumours. It's just quiet-season speculation."
Under the constitution, the president has the right to dissolve the National Assembly at any time once it has been elected for 12 months. The legislature's normal term is five years.
Officials recalled that Chirac has said repeatedly that a dissolution was not a matter of personal convenience and would only be justified to settle a political crisis.

Opinion polls in the last month have shown support for the ruling centre-right coalition edging back up to about 40 percent while support for the main opposition Socialist party has slipped about four points to 26 percent.
Projections based on those figures suggested the conservatives would be re-elected with a comfortable, but reduced majority. They currently hold 480 of the 577 seats.
Liberation said the secretary-general of Chirac's Gaullist RPR party, Jean-Francois Mancel, who is close to Juppe, was pressing for an early election.
But it quoted a Chirac aide as saying the president was "very, very reserved" about the idea.
Talk of a dissolution, or a cabinet reshuffle, was rife in the corridors of parliament before the National Assembly took an Easter break last week.
Le Monde noted that the ruling coalition parties had virtually completed selecting their candidates and were thus ready for an election.

Other pointers cited are the fact that a successful June election could give Chirac a parliamentary majority for the rest of his seven-year term, removing the risk of power-sharing with the left-wing opposition.
It would also avoid any possible collision between the election timetable and European Union plans to select early next year the countries that qualify for a single European currency in 1999.
